Korn’s inequality asserts the control of the $L^2$ norm of the gradient of a vector field by the $L^2$ norm of its symmetric part, under certain conditions.
Introduction Let $\Omega$ be a smooth bounded open set in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $d \ge 2$ to avoid trivial situations. For a vector field $u: \Omega ightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$, we denote by $
abla u$ the differential of $u$ with values in $\mathfrak{M}$ where $\mathfrak{M}$ is the set of $d 	imes d$ real matrices. We also denote by $
abla^su$ (resp. $
abla^a u$) the symmetric (resp. antisymmetric) part of $
abla u$ that takes values in $\mathfrak{M}^s$ (resp. $\mathfrak{M}^a$) where $\mathfrak{M}^s$ (resp. $\mathfrak{M}^a$) is the set of $d 	imes d$ real symmetric (resp. antisymmetric) matrices. Written with Cartesian coordinates, this mean that
$$ (
abla u)_{ij} =  rac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j}, \quad (
abla^su)_{ij} =  rac{1}{2}\left( rac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j} +  rac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i}ight), \quad (
abla^a u)_{ij} =  rac{1}{2}\left( rac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j} -  rac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i}ight). $$Moreover, when $u = (u_j)$ and $M = (m_{ij})$ are respectively a vector field and a matrix field on $\Omega$, we use the following notations,
$$ \|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)} = \left(\int_{\Omega}|u|^pight)^{1/p},\quad \|M\|_{L^p(\Omega)} = \left(\int_{\Omega}|M|^pight)^{1/p}, $$where
$$ |u| = \left(\sum_{j} u_j^2ight)^{1/2},\quad |M| = \left(\sum_{ij}m_{ij}^2ight)^{1/2}. $$The core of this note is the inequality of the following form:
$$ \|
abla u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 \le C(\Omega)\|
abla^su\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2, 	ag{H0} $$where $C(\Omega) > 0$ is a constant that depends only on the domain $\Omega$.
Application in the mechanics of elastic solid The theory of elasticity seeks to answer a fundamental question:
How does a solid body resist deformation and return to its original configuration once the external forces are removed?
In the regime of small deformations, this behavor is described by the Hooke’s law, which asserts that the restoring force depends linearly on the displacement. This linear relation admits a local formulation in terms of stress (internal forces per unit area) and strain (local deformation). The elastic energy arises from the work done by internal forces during deformation; for a linear elastic body, this work is path-independent and leads to an elastic energy given by a quadratic form of the strain.
We now make the above description more precise from a mathematical point of view. The deformation of a body is described by a displacement field $u = u(x)$ which assigns to each reference point $x$ its new position. The gradient of the displacement $
abla u$ encodes the local behavior of deformation; however, it also includes contributions from rigid-body rotations.
More precisely, since any square matrix can be decomposed into its symmetric and antisymmetric parts, we write
$$ 
abla u = 
abla^su + 
abla^a u. $$The symmetric part $
abla^su$, called the strain tensor, accounts for the deformation (stretching, compression, and shear) which modify the size and shape of an infinitesimal element. It is this component that gives rise to the stress that describes forces present during deformation and leads to the storage of elastic energy. In contrast, the antisymmetric part $
abla^au$, called the spin tensor, represents the rate of rotation, which does not change the shape of the body and hence does not contribute to the elastic energy.
In general, the elastic energy associated with a displacement field $u$ is given by
$$ \mathcal{E}(u) = \int_{\Omega} \mathcal{W}(u)\mathrm{d}x, $$where $\mathcal{W} : \mathbb{R}^d ightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is the elastic energy density. In the linear regime, the energy density can be expressed as
$$ \mathcal{W}(u) =  rac{1}{2} \sigma(u) : 
abla^s u, $$In a homogeneous and isotropic body, the stress tensor is given by
$$ \sigma(u) = 2\mu 
abla^su + \lambda(\operatorname{tr}
abla^s u) I. 	ag{1} $$where $\mu > 0$ measures resistance to shear, and $\lambda > 0$ measures resistance to expansion or compression. A simple computation yields
$$ \mathcal{E}(u) = \mu \int_{\Omega} |
abla^s u|^2\mathrm{d}x +  rac{\lambda}{2} \int_{\Omega}|\operatorname{tr}
abla^su|^2\mathrm{d}x. 	ag{2} $$This means that the elastic energy $\mathcal{E}(u)$ provides the control only on the symmetric part $
abla^su$ of the gradient, namely,
$$ C\|
abla^su\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 \le \mathcal{E}(u). 	ag{3} $$However, the regularity and stability of displacement field $u$ are measured in terms of the full gradient $
abla u$, for instance, through the $H^1$ norm. To address this issue, we need an estimate that allows to recover control of $
abla u$ from $
abla^s u$, that is, the inequality (H0).
Application in the mechanics of fluid In fluid dynamics, we seeks to describe the evolution of a velocity field $u = u(x,t)$, which represents the motion of a fluid. The fundamental equations governing viscous flows, such as the Navier-Stokes equations, combine transport effects with internal forces generated by viscosity. For Newtonian fluids, these internal forces re described by the viscous stress tensor, defined again by (1). In this context, $\mu > 0$ is called the dynamic viscosity, while $\lambda > 0$ is called the bulk viscosity. As in elasticity, the stress depends only on the symmetric part $
abla^s u$ of the gradient. The rate of energy dissipation due to viscosity is given by (2). This implies that the dissipation provides control only on $
abla^su$ according to (3). Therefore, we are led to look for an inequality (H0) to get the regularity and stability of the velocity field $u$.
Korn-type inequalities Unfortunately, the inequality (H0) is not true for all the vector fields. Consider a rigid motion
$$ u(x) = Ax + b, $$where $A \in \mathfrak{M}^a$ is an antisymmetric constant matrix and $b \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a constant vector. The gradient $
abla u$ of u is equal to $A$, while its symmetric part $
abla^s u$ vanishes. As a consequence, the inequality (H0) can not hold for such rigid motions.
The key idea to eliminate this degeneracy, proposed by the mathematician Arthur Korn, is to either impose suitable boundary conditions that exclude rigid motions, or to work modulo rigid motions. We next briefly review Korn’s results and some variants.
Korn’s first inequality states that, there exists a constant $C_{K1}(\Omega) > 0$ such that for all vector fields $u : \Omega ightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ with $u|_{\partial\Omega} = 0$ where $\partial\Omega$ is the boundary of $\Omega$, it holds
$$ \|
abla u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\le C_{K1}(\Omega) \|
abla^su\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. 	ag{H1} $$Instead of imposing boundary condition, Korn’s second inequality holds by work modulo rigid motions. Let $\mathcal{R}(\Omega)$ be the finite-dimensional set of all rigid motions on $\Omega$, there exists a constant $C_{K2}(\Omega) > 0$ such that for all vector fields $u:\Omegaightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$,
$$ \inf\limits_{R\in\mathcal{R}(\Omega)}\|
abla(u - R)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 \le C_{K2}(\Omega)\|
abla^su\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. 	ag{H2} $$Some well-known variants are the following:
$$ \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 + \|
abla u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 \le C_K'(\Omega)\left(\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|
abla^s u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2ight). $$and
$$ \inf\limits_{R\in\mathcal{R}(\Omega)}\|
abla(u - R)\|_{L^q(\Omega)} \le C_K''(\Omega)\|
abla^su\|_{L^p(\Omega)}, $$for any $1 \le p < \infty$, $p 
eq d$, $q = dp/(d-p)$ ($q = \infty$ if $p > d$).
Proof of Korn’s second inequality Let us here briefly recall an elegant and robust proof of (H2) based on an argument of Jacques-Louis Lions according to the statements in [3].
Sobolev spaces Before the proof, we shall recall fundamental knowledge of function spaces. The Sobolev space $H_0^1(\Omega)$ is defined as the closure of smooth compactly supported functions with respect to the $H^1$ norm, namely,
$$ f \in H_0^1(\Omega) \iff \exists f_n\in C_c^\infty(\Omega),\quad f_n ightarrow f \;	ext{in}\; H^1(\Omega). $$If $\partial\Omega$ is regular enough, it can be interpreted as the set of functions that vanish on the boundary,
$$ H_0^1(\Omega) = \left\{f\in H^1(\Omega)\,;\, f|_{\partial\Omega} = 0 ight\}. $$The space $H^{-1}(\Omega)$ is defined as the dual space of $H_0^1(\Omega)$, namely, the space of continuous linear functionals on $H_0^1(\Omega)$. The standard dual norm of $u \in H^{-1}(\Omega)$ reads
$$ \|f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)} = \sup\left\{\int_{\Omega}f\varphi\,;\, \varphi \in H_0^1(\Omega),\|\varphi\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le 1ight\}. $$The Poincaré inequality tells us that for all $f \in H_0^1(\Omega)$,
$$ \|
abla f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 \le \|f\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2 \le (1+C_P^2)\|
abla f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$Since $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is dense in $H_0^1(\Omega)$, an equivalent form of $H^{-1}$ norm is given by
$$ \|f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)} = \sup\left\{|\int_{\Omega}f\varphi|\,;\, \varphi \in C_c^\infty(\Omega),\|
abla\varphi\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le 1ight\}. $$There is another very useful equivalent characterization of the $H^{-1}$ norm. For $f \in H^{-1}(\Omega)$, define $\phi$ as the solution in $H_0^1(\Omega)$ of the Laplace problem on $\Omega$, i.e.,
$$ -\Delta\phi = f, \quad \phi|_{\partial\Omega} = 0. $$By a standard Lax-Milgram argument, there exists a bijective operator $\Delta^{-1}$ that maps $ f \in H^{-1}(\Omega)$ to $\phi \in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Using integration by parts, we can verify the following proposition.
Proposition 1. The $H^{-1}$ norm of $f$ is equivalent to the $L^2$ norm of $
abla\Delta^{-1}f$.
The Lions lemma [4, Theorem 3.2] states that
$$ L^2(\Omega) = \left\{f \in H^{-1}(\Omega)\,;\, 
abla f \in [H^{-1}(\Omega)]^dight\}. $$Moreover, Duvant and Lions have shown the following inequality in [4, Remark 3.1]:
$$ \|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \le C\left(\|f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)} + \|
abla f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)}ight), $$where
$$ \|
abla f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^d\|\partial_i f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)}ight)^{1/2}. $$Poincaré–Lions inquality We introduce the notation
$$ \langle fangle =  rac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}f, $$where $|\Omega|$ stands for the volume of $\Omega$. In [3], Desvillettes and Villani present a strong lemma that involves a Poincaré-type inequality with respect to the $H^{-1}$ norm of $
abla f$. We will review this lemma and its proof here.
Lemma 2. There exists a constant $C(\Omega)$ such that for all $f \in L^2(\Omega)$, $$ \|
abla f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)}^2 \le d\|f - \langle fangle\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 \le C(\Omega)\|
abla f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)}^2. $$ Proof of Lemma 2. Regarding the first inequality, for each $f \in L^2(\Omega)$, we have $\partial_i f \in H^{-1}(\Omega)$ and then by Cauchy-Schwartz inequality
$$ (\partial_i f)(\varphi) = -\int_{\Omega}f \partial_i \varphi \le \|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\|\partial_i\varphi\|_{L^2(\Omega)},\quad  orall \varphi \in C_c^\infty(\Omega). $$This implies that for all $1 \le i \le d$, $$ \|\partial_i f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)} \le \|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}. $$Then, for each $f \in L^2(\Omega)$, we have $f - \langle fangle \in L^2(\Omega)$ due to the boundedness of $\Omega$ and
$$ \|
abla f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{d}\|\partial_i f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{d}\|\partial_i (f-\langle fangle)\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)}^2\le d\|f-\langle fangle\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$For the second inequality, we present a proof based on the closed graph theorem. We denote by $X$ the set of all functions in $L^2(\Omega)$ of which the mean is zero, namely,
$$ X = \left\{f \in L^2(\Omega)\,;\, \langle fangle = 0ight\}, $$and $Y = [H^{-1}(\Omega)]^d$. Define the linear operator $T: X ightarrow Y$ by $(Tf)_i = \partial_i f$ for all $1 \le i \le d$. First, $T$ is injective on $X$. Indeed, let $f \in X$ and $Tf = 0$, then by definition $f$ is a constant. Since $\langle fangle = 0$, we have $f = 0$. Second, we denote by $Z$ the range of $T$ and define the inverse $T^{-1}: Z \subset Y ightarrow X$ by $T^{-1}(
abla f) = f$. For a sequence $(g_n) = (
abla f_n) \subset Z $ that converges to $g \in Y$ and another sequence $(T^{-1}(g_n)) = (f_n) \subset X$ that converges to $f \in X$, we want to show that $g = 
abla f$. Indeed, for every test function $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and $ 1 \le i \le d$, we have
$$ g_{n,i}(\varphi) = (\partial_i f_n)(\varphi) = -\int_{\Omega} f_n\partial_i\varphi. $$Taking the limit $n ightarrow +\infty$ gives
$$ g_i(\varphi) = - \lim\limits_{nightarrow +\infty}\int_{\Omega} f_n\partial_i\varphi = - \int_{\Omega} (\lim\limits_{nightarrow +\infty}f_n)\partial_i\varphi = - \int_{\Omega} f\partial_i\varphi = (\partial_i f)(\varphi). $$This implies $g = 
abla f$ and hence the graph of $T^{-1}$ is closed in $Z 	imes X$. By the closed graph theorem, $T^{-1}$ is bounded. Therefore, there exists a constant $C(\Omega) > 0$ such that for all $g \in Z$,
$$ \|T^{-1}g\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \le C(\Omega)\|g\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)}. $$Since $T^{-1}$ is surjective on $X$, we deduce that for all $f \in L^2(\Omega)$,
$$ \|f - \langle fangle\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \le C(\Omega)\|
abla f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)}. $$$$ \phantom{.}	ag*{$\square$} $$ Remark 1. Desvillettes and Villani also mentioned another simple and constructive proof provided by Meyer for the second inquality in Lemma 2. We refer to [3] for more details.
Schwarz theorem The following lemma allows us to write all the components of the second-order differential of a vector field $u$ in terms of its symmetric part of the gradient.
Lemma 3. Let $u : \Omega ightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ be a vector field in $[H^1(\Omega)]^d$. Then, for all $1\le i,j,k\le d$, $$ \partial_k(
abla^a u)_{ij} = \partial_j(
abla^su)_{ik} - \partial_i(
abla^su)_{jk}. $$ This algebraic property is at the core of all Korn’s type inequalities. It implies that the derivatives of $
abla^au$ are linear combinations of the derivatives of $
abla^su$.
The optimal rigid motion Lemma 4. Let $u : \Omega ightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ be a vector field in $[H^1(\Omega)]^d$, then $$ \|
abla u-\langle
abla^auangle\|_{L^2(\Omega)} = \inf\limits_{R\in\mathcal{R}(\Omega)} \|
abla(u-R)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}. $$ Proof of Lemma 4. For any rigid motion $R(x) = Ax + b$ with $A \in \mathfrak{M}^a$, we have
$$ \|
abla(u - R)\|_{L^2(\Omega)} = \|
abla u - A\|_{L^2(\Omega)} = \|
abla^s u + 
abla^a u - A\|_{L^2(\Omega)}. $$Since the symmetric matrix and antiasymmetric matrices are orthogonal in the Frobenius product, we get
$$ \|
abla(u - R)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 = \|
abla^s u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 + \|
abla^a u - A\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$Therefore, the minimization reduces to
$$ \inf\limits_{A\in\mathfrak{M}^a}\|
abla^au - A\|_{L^2(\Omega)}. $$This is just the best approximation of $
abla^au$ by a constant antisymmetric matrix. The minimier is its mean value:
$$ A_* = \langle
abla^auangle =  rac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}
abla^au. $$Indeed, for any $A \in \mathfrak{M}^a$,
$$ 
abla^a u - A = (
abla^au - \langle
abla^auangle) + (\langle
abla^auangle - A). $$The first term has zero mean, while the second is constant. Hence they are orthogonal in $L^2(\Omega)$, and
$$ \|
abla^au - A\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 = \|
abla^au - \langle
abla^auangle\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 + |\Omega||\langle
abla^auangle - A|^2. $$The minimum is attained when $A = \langle 
abla^auangle$, which completes the proof.
$$ \phantom{.}	ag*{$\square$} $$Main proof Now we turn to the proof of the Korn’s second inequlity (H2) based on the above preliminary results. By the Lemma 4, (H2) is equivalent to
$$ \|
abla^a u - \langle
abla^auangle\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 \le C_{K2}\|
abla^su\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$By the second inequality in Lemma 2, we have
$$ \|
abla^a u - \langle
abla^auangle\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 \le C\|
abla
abla^a u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$By the Lemma 3, $
abla
abla^au$ is a matrix combination of $
abla
abla^su$. Hence, using the first inequality in Lemma 2 and the triangle inequality, we derive the inequality (H2).
$$ \phantom{.}	ag*{$\square$} $$References [1] Wikipedia.
[2] SciencePedia.
[3] Laurent Desvillettes and Cédric Villani, On a variant of Korn’s inequality arising in statistical mechanics, ESAIM: Control, Optimisation and Calculus of Variations 8 (2002) 603–619.
[4] Georges Duvaut and Jacques Louis Lions, Inequalities in Mechanics and Physics, vol. 219, Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften, Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg, 1976.
[5] Kleber Carrapatoso, Jean Dolbeault, Frédéric Hérau, Stéphane Mischler, and Clément Mouhot, Weighted Korn and Poincaré-Korn Inequalities in the Euclidean Space and Associated Operators, Archive for Rational Mechanics and Analysis 243 no. 3 (2022) 1565–1596.
summary: Korn’s inequality asserts the control of the $L^2$ norm of the gradient of a vector field by the $L^2$ norm of its symmetric part, under certain conditions.
title: Korn's Inequality

A major update in Windows 11 is to provide WSL2 as a more efficient and elegant solution for running Linux on Windows. By utilizing a lightweight utility virtual machine and a real Linux kernel, WSL2 bridges the gap between Windows productivity and Linux development power, providing nearly 100% system call compatibility. This note records how I set up my personal development environment in WSL2.
WSL2 + WSLg WSL stands for Windows Subsystem for Linux; the suffixes “2” and “g” correspond to the version number and GUI support, respectively. It is worth noting that WSL1 and WSL2 use completely different technical approaches; I personally recommend using WSL2.
For installation of WSL2 and WSLg, please refer to the official tutorial.
Windows Terminal Windows Terminal offers a more visually appealing terminal interface. The theme settings I use are as follows:
"colorScheme": "One Half Dark", "useAcrylic": true, "acrylicOpacity": 0.8 To resolve the green highlighting issue with the ls command, please refer to this link.
Oh My Zsh Oh My Zsh is a visually appealing terminal theme. For specific configuration details, please refer to this post.
Note: The configuration file for zsh is ~/.zshrc, while the configuration file for bash is ~/.bashrc.
Git Git is a free and open-source distributed version control system widely used by software developers. Since Ubuntu comes with the appropriate version of Git pre-installed, we generally do not need to download it manually.
GitHub is a cloud-based developer platform used to create, store, manage, and share code repositories.
To use Git in the subsystem and link it to a GitHub account, we simply need to configure the SSH server. The specific steps are as follows.
Step 1: Generate an SSH key. Please refer to the official tutorial. Step 2: Add the SSH key to your GitHub account settings. VIM VIM is a highly customizable text editor. We can tailor it to our personal preferences. The default configuration file of VIM is ~/.vimrc; the key to customization is creating your own .vimrc file.
In addition to basic configuration, we can use package managers (such as Vundle) to download and manage various plugins.
Note: Performing a comprehensive configuration yourself usually consumes a lot of time and effort, especially regarding themes and development environments. Therefore, I recommend setting up your own familiar keyboard shortcuts and then using VIM plugins within other mature text editors (such as Visual Studio Code).
Visual Studio Code Visual Studio Code (VsCode) is a cross-platform integrated development environment (IDE) released by Microsoft. To use VsCode in a subsystem, you first need to download and install it on the main Windows system, then follow the official documentation to configure remote control for the subsystem.
Gnuplot Gnuplot is a simple yet powerful command-line plotting tool. To install it on an Ubuntu system, simply run the following commands:
sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install gnuplot For usage of this tool, please refer to the official documentation.
summary: A major update in Windows 11 is to provide WSL2 as a more efficient and elegant solution for running Linux on Windows. By utilizing a lightweight utility virtual machine and a real Linux kernel, WSL2 bridges the gap between Windows productivity and Linux development power, providing nearly 100% system call compatibility. This note records how I set up my personal development environment in WSL2.
title: Use Linux in Windows: Subsystem
